title: A Tesla Flying Car? I Don’t Know, Man
gist: Tesla demoed a Roadster 2 prototype that hopped a few dozen feet at SpaceX's Texas site, but aviation experts say FAA certification, pilot licensing, state rules and the weight-versus-flight physics make a true flying car a long way off; production is slated for 2028.

insights.claim: Tesla showed a Roadster 2 prototype that flew a few dozen feet unoccupied at SpaceX's McGregor, Texas facility; the car has no price yet, is likely very expensive, and is slated for production in 2028.
insights.speaker: Aarian Marshall
insights.so_what: Ties the long-delayed Roadster to a 2028 production claim, a milestone to monitor.

insights.claim: Musk acknowledged the car may not be legal in all jurisdictions and is not necessarily safety-optimized.
insights.speaker: Aarian Marshall
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk is admitted by the company itself.
insights.quote: This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car.
insights.locator: At the event Thursday, Musk acknowledged

insights.claim: The FAA has jurisdiction over any machine that leaves the ground, and a flying vehicle over roughly 250 pounds needs FAA approval that former FAA official Michael McCormick predicts could take at least a year, plus a recreational aviation license for owners.
insights.speaker: Aarian Marshall
insights.so_what: Certification timelines and licensing limit near-term addressable demand for a roadable aircraft.
insights.locator: Any flying vehicle that weighs more than 250

insights.claim: State and local rules typically require aircraft to take off from airports or helipads, so a road-launched flying car might only operate on large private land.
insights.speaker: Aarian Marshall
insights.so_what: Operational limits shrink the use case to niche buyers.
insights.locator: Actually taking off and landing the Roadster 2

insights.claim: The FAA is working on rules and a limited three-year Trump administration pilot for eVTOL aircraft, which carry up to four passengers 20 to 150 miles from vertipads; companies have waited years for certification.
insights.speaker: Aarian Marshall
insights.so_what: The eVTOL certification path is the more realistic regulated 'flying car' market.
insights.locator: The FAA today is working on rules

insights.claim: True flying cars have struggled because road safety and durability require weight, which is the enemy of aircraft; no one has found the balance of power versus weight.
insights.speaker: Aarian Marshall
insights.so_what: Skeptical base case for any roadable-aircraft product timeline.
insights.quote: weight is the enemy of an airplane,
insights.locator: When it comes to the Roadster 2
